name: Stanozolol

lead: Stanozolol (Winstrol) is an anabolic steroid approved for hereditary angioedema and used in animals. Bodybuilders use it for lean, dry muscle, and it became famous through the 1988 Ben Johnson doping case.
No controlled trial tests it for appearance in healthy people. Teen forum posters ask about it for height, and no studies support that use.

paras: It activates the androgen receptor and, in angioedema, raises production of C1 inhibitor in the liver. Its 17-alpha-alkyl structure lets it be taken orally.

A weight-lifter study found oral stanozolol cut HDL cholesterol sharply; case reports and animal data describe liver injury, and reviews link AAS to cardiac deaths. It is US Schedule III and prohibited in sport.

lead: Stanozolol, known by the brand name Winstrol, is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid (AAS) derived from dihydrotestosterone. It was developed in the early 1960s, is approved in the United States for prophylaxis of hereditary angioedema, and is also used in veterinary medicine.[1] It is available as an oral tablet and as an injectable preparation.[1]

Outside medicine it is used by athletes and bodybuilders for lean muscle, strength and a dry, defined look, and it became widely known through doping cases, notably the 1988 Olympic disqualification of sprinter Ben Johnson (per an encyclopedic overview).[1] It is one of the most frequently detected anabolic agents in anti-doping testing.[1]

Controlled research on its appearance effects is sparse. Documented studies concern effects on blood lipids in weight lifters, safety signals such as liver injury, and medical uses in angioedema and blood disorders. In looksmaxxing forums it appears mainly in threads by teenagers asking about height, a use for which no supporting studies were found.
infobox: US Schedule III; prohibited in sport

paras: Stanozolol is used to prevent attacks in hereditary angioedema, where it increases hepatic production of C1 inhibitor and complement component C4.[1] Other human uses have included aplastic anaemia, osteoporosis and some vascular conditions, though these have largely declined.[1] A clinical study evaluated it after decitabine treatment in high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome.[2] In veterinary practice it has been used to improve appetite and weight in dogs, cats and horses.[1]

Bodybuilders use it to build lean mass without much water retention, often in cutting phases.[1] A 1989 study examined its use among competitive bodybuilders as part of surveys of AAS incidence.[3] In looksmaxxing forums posters ask about stacking Winstrol with other compounds to masculinise the face and physique or while 'heightmaxing'.[4][5][6]

Stanozolol is a 17-alpha-alkylated DHT derivative, a structure that permits oral use and is associated with liver strain.[1] Its binding to androgen receptors in skeletal muscle and prostate was compared with other anabolic steroids in a 1984 study.[7]

A 1989 JAMA crossover study gave 11 male weight lifters oral stanozolol or intramuscular testosterone enanthate for six weeks. Stanozolol reduced HDL cholesterol sharply, while testosterone had a different effect, supporting the view that oral administration is a key factor in the lipid change.[8] Earlier work examined reductions of lipoprotein(a) with stanozolol.[9] A 2010 study of weight lifters taking Decadurabolin and Winstrol for two months reported chromosome damage and cytotoxicity in oral mucosa cells.[10]

A 1977 controlled study examined long-term anabolic therapy in the elderly,[11] and a clinical study in myelodysplastic syndrome reported improved progression-free survival when added to decitabine maintenance.[2] No controlled trial of stanozolol for cosmetic muscle gain in healthy people was found.

Stanozolol is associated with liver injury; a case report described stanozolol-induced bland cholestasis,[12] and a trial in cats reported hepatotoxicity.[13] The lipid effect noted above, a large reduction in HDL cholesterol, is a recognised cardiovascular concern.[8] A review of sudden cardiac death in AAS users covers cardiac mechanisms across the drug class.[14] Reviewed medical use also notes menstrual irregularities in women at maintenance doses (encyclopedic source).[1]

Stanozolol is a US Schedule III controlled substance and is banned in sport; the 1988 Ben Johnson case is its best-known doping scandal.[1] Supplements have also been found cross-contaminated or faked with doping agents.[15] T Nation users note that prescriptions at supraphysiological doses of drugs like stanozolol are a legal grey area.[16]
